display.title: The Gilgul in the Wheat: Rabbi Levi Yitzchak and the Missing Brachah
display.summary_short: A stranger drinks a l'chaim without a brachah, and Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev tells him of a soul that waited in a grain of wheat for someone to make a brachah.
display.summary_long: A stranger who has not davened in years rushes into a village shul to say Kaddish on his father's yahrzeit. When he brings a l'chaim for the congregation and drinks it himself without a brachah, there is an uproar, and Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev sits him down for a story. Reuven, a kind but unlearned Jew, passes away and comes before the Heavenly Court. One by one, angels of his mitzvos and his sins climb onto the scale: a penny to a poor man, eating his mother's supper with a brachah, lending a pencil, giving in instead of fighting, and on the other side a lie, a theft, lashon hara and forgetting negel vasser. The scale ends exactly even, so a spark of his soul is sent down in a raindrop that grows into a stalk of wheat, is harvested, cooked into vodka and set on the shelf of this very village's store, waiting for someone to make a brachah over it. That soul, says Rabbi Levi Yitzchak, was the stranger's father. Shaken, the man does teshuvah, learns Torah with the Rebbe and becomes a learned Chassid, and his teshuvah lifts his father's soul to Gan Eden. The storyteller adds why every brachah matters.
display.lesson: Always say a brachah before eating or drinking; it is Hashem's 'payment' and it elevates the food, and sincere teshuvah can repair even a missed mitzvah.

advisories.note: A soul is judged in the Heavenly Court, Gehinnom is mentioned, and the soul returns in a grain of wheat (gilgul).
An old man passes away peacefully; his son is observing his yahrzeit.
A l'chaim of vodka in shul; the grain is made into vodka.
